system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2182-07-31 02:31:00 to 2182-08-07 18:41:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with stage IV cholangiocarcinoma, was admitted with recurrent fevers and found to have acute cholecystitis with a contained gallbladder rupture. He underwent percutaneous cholecystostomy tube placement, which drained purulent material. Post-procedure, he developed fevers, rigors, and a lactate of 5.5, consistent with severe sepsis, and was transferred to the ICU. Blood and gallbladder cultures confirmed E. coli infection, which showed intermediate sensitivity to meropenem. Antibiotics were switched to tigecycline, and a PICC line was placed for outpatient IV therapy. His condition improved with treatment, and he was discharged home to complete a 7-day course of tigecycline, with follow-up arranged for drain management and oncology care.

radiology_notes.text:
EXAMINATION:  CONTRAST ENHANCED CT ABDOMEN AND PELVIS

INDICATION:  Cholangiocarcinoma with biliary stents and recent gallbladder
rupture causing sepsis and requiring percutaneous cholecystostomy. Now
presenting with fevers and fatigue. Evaluate for cholangitis.

TECHNIQUE:  Axial MDCT images were obtained through the abdomen and pelvis
after the uneventful administration of IV contrast. No oral contrast was
provided. Sagittal and coronal reformats were generated.

TOTAL EXAM DLP: 682 MGy-cm.

COMPARISON:  Prior abdominal/ pelvic CT from ___.

FINDINGS: 

There is bibasilar linear atelectasis. No pleural or pericardial effusion
identified.
CT of the abdomen: There is redemonstration of a pigtail cholecystostomy tube
in the right upper quadrant, in unchanged position as compared to prior exam
from ___. Again the tube takes a transhepatic course and there is no
new fluid collection surrounding the tube or the gallbladder fossa.
Low-density material surrounding the gallbladder fossa is again seen, likley
inflammatory changes,  not significantly increased since prior. Fluid and
stranding along the colon has decreased since prior examination. There is no
new drainable collection seen within the liver. There is no subcapsular
hematoma. The portal vein is patent.
The patient has bilateral metallic biliary stents with 1 extending into the
left lobe of the liver. The right-sided stent again extends to the posterior
ducts on the right which are slightly more dilated as compared to prior. A
separate internal external drainage courses centrally via the left-sided stent
and again loops back on itself. There is expected pneumobilia, similar in
appearance to prior examination.
The adrenal glands and pancreas are normal. The spleen is enlarged measuring
15 cm. Note is made of accessory spleens. The left kidney contains a 10 mm
hypodensity at the lower pole, likely a cyst. The kidneys otherwise enhance
symmetrically and excrete contrast without evidence of hydronephrosis or renal
masses.
The stomach is collapsed. There is no small bowel obstruction. There are
sigmoid diverticula with no evidence of acute diverticulitis. The appendix is
not clearly visualized, however there is no evidence of acute appendicitis.
Small and large bowel are otherwise grossly unremarkable. There is no free
fluid. There is no free air.
CT of the pelvis: The urinary bladder and terminal ureters are normal. The
prostate is mildly enlarged. There is no pelvic free fluid. There is no
inguinal or pelvic lymph node enlargement by CT size criteria.
Osseous structures: No blastic or lytic lesion concerning for malignancy

IMPRESSION: 

1. No new fluid collection identified within the liver. Intrahepatic biliary
ducts are slightly more dilated on the right as compared to prior.
2. Unchanged positioning of biliary stents and internal-external biliary drain
which is coiled on itself in the distal end of the left metal stent.

NOTIFICATION:  Initial findings discussed with Dr. ___ In person at 340
AM. Discussed with ___ by NSR the telephone on ___ at
4:23AM.

EXAMINATION:  LIVER OR GALLBLADDER US (SINGLE ORGAN)

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with cholangiocarcinoma and multiple biliary
stents s/p ERCP  // assess for interval change in dilatation after ERCP

TECHNIQUE:  Grey scale and color Doppler ultrasound images of the abdomen were
obtained.

COMPARISON:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

LIVER: The left lobe liver is not well evaluated due to obscuration by
overlying gas. Right lobe of the liver demonstrates normal echogenicity with
smooth contours. There is no ascites.

BILE DUCTS:  A percutaneous drain is partially visualized traversing the right
lobe of the liver. Left intrahepatic biliary ducts and common bile duct are
not visualized. There is mild prominence of the intrahepatic biliary ducts in
the right lobe, similar to comparison CT.

GALLBLADDER: The gallbladder is obscured by overlying gas.

PANCREAS: Visualized portions of the pancreatic head and body are within
normal limits without mass or pancreatic duct dilatation. The pancreatic tail
is obscured by overlying gas.

SPLEEN:  The spleen is enlarged, measuring 16.5 cm in length. A 1.6 cm
accessory spleen is incidentally noted near the tail of the pancreas.

IMPRESSION: 

1.  Poor visualization of left intrahepatic bile ducts due to overlying gas.
No evidence of increased biliary dilatation within the right hepatic lobe.
2.  Mild splenomegaly.

EXAMINATION:  CHEST PORT. LINE PLACEMENT

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with new picc  // L picc 50 cm ___ ___ 
Contact name: ___: ___     L picc 50 cm ___ ___

IMPRESSION: 

In comparison with the study of ___, there are lower lung volumes with
extensive atelectatic changes at the bases.  Otherwise, no change except for
placement of a left subclavian PICC line extends to the mid portion of the
SVC.

INDICATION:  ___ year old man with cholangiocarcinoma c/b GB rupture and GNR
sepsis, now s/p ERCP  // Eval for interval change s/p ERCP

TECHNIQUE:  The patient was brought to the fluoroscopy suite and placed supine
on the imaging table.  Scout radiographs of the abdomen were obtained before
this examination. Using sterile technique, the existing pigtail
cholecystostomy tube was on catheter and 25 cc of water-soluble contrast was
hand injected until resistance was met.

COMPARISON:  ___ CT abdomen pelvis.

FINDINGS: 

Contrast accumulates in the expected location of the gallbladder.  No drainage
into the CBD or intestine is identified. Contrast leak was identified into the
right mid-abdominal peritoneal cavity along the course of the cholecystostomy
tube.  No external contrast leak was identified.

After the exam, the cholecystostomy tube was placed to bag drainage. No
complications during or immediately after this exam.

IMPRESSION: 

Injected contrast does not drain into the CBD or small intestine. Retrograde
contrast leak identified into the right peritoneal cavity along the course of
the cholecystostomy tube becuase of the cystic duct obstruction and the
injection technique.

NOTIFICATION:   The findings were discussed via telephone by Dr. ___ with Dr.
___ on ___ at 6:01 ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You're here because of abdominal pain and fevers. We’re concerned this might be another episode of cholangitis, especially given your history of cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the pain in my right side has been getting worse, and I’ve had chills all night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your CT scan from earlier today. It shows your biliary stents are still in place, but the bile ducts on the right side look more dilated than before, which suggests a blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I’m so sick again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The blockage can cause bile to back up and get infected—this is cholangitis. We’ve started broad-spectrum antibiotics because you’ve had resistant bacteria before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time—it was E. coli, right? And it didn’t respond well to regular antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. So we’re starting you on a combination that covers resistant organisms. We’ll narrow it down once we get blood culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the drain I have? It’s been draining green fluid like usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s your biliary drain, and the green bile is normal. We’ll keep monitoring the output. We also need to check if your gallbladder drain is working properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling nauseous and vomited once last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added ondansetron for nausea. That should help. We’ll keep an eye on your labs too—your liver enzymes and bilirubin are elevated, which fits with bile duct obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be here this time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It depends on how quickly you respond to antibiotics and whether we need a procedure. We’re planning an ERCP to look at the blockage and possibly clear it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It’s not too bad. When would it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve scheduled it for tomorrow morning. In the meantime, we’ll keep you on IV fluids and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. We’re getting ready for your ERCP. The goal is to open up the blocked bile duct and make sure your stents are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put in a new stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. The radiology team will decide based on what they see. You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP went well. They found your stent was partially blocked, and they cleared it. No new stent was needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. Do you think that’ll help with the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, relieving the blockage is key. Now the bile can drain properly, which should help the antibiotics work better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My pain is already a little better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll keep monitoring your temperature and repeat blood work to see how you’re responding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound yesterday to check the bile ducts. The right side doesn’t look more dilated, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the spleen? I remember they said it was big.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s mildly enlarged, but that’s been stable. It’s not a concern right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My stomach’s been a little off—any chance it’s C. diff again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool, and it was positive. So we’re starting you on oral vancomycin to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, I remember that helped last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures have come back negative for growth so far. That’s a good sign—no bacteria in the blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks that way. We’re going to place a PICC line today so you can finish IV antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that be uncomfortable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a quick procedure with local anesthesia. You’ll have it in your arm and it’ll allow a nurse to give your antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line is in and working well. Chest X-ray confirms it’s positioned correctly in the superior vena cava.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’d like to get home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re on track for discharge in a few days. We need to make sure your infection is fully controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your blood cultures are negative now—no growth after 48 hours. That means the bacteremia has cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your liver function tests are also improving—bilirubin is down to 0.5 and enzymes are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the antibiotics? How long do I need them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish a 14-day course from the time your blood cultures turned negative. That means about two more weeks of IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the vancomycin for C. diff?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish that too—another week should do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. A visiting nurse will come to your home to give the IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to take care of my drains, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Empty the drainage bag daily and record the amount. Change the dressing every three days using sterile water or half-strength hydrogen peroxide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I flush the drain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, do not flush it. If the flow slows or the site becomes painful or red, call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my pain meds—I’ll keep taking them as before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue your regular pain medications. We’ve added mirtazapine at night to help with appetite and sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’ve been a little down lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are stable. White count is still low but improving. We’re comfortable discharging you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your oncologist and the interventional radiology team to manage your drains. We’ll send the details to your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the DNR status—I want to make sure that’s still in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your DNR status is documented and will be communicated to all providers involved in your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. You’re cleared to go home. The nurse will review your medications and drain care one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve responded well. Keep taking the IV antibiotics as scheduled, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to write down the drain output every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson was admitted with abdominal pain and fevers due to recurrent cholangitis in the setting of stage IV cholangiocarcinoma and biliary stents. Imaging showed biliary duct dilation suggesting obstruction. He underwent ERCP which cleared a blocked stent, relieving the obstruction. He was treated for bacteremia with broad-spectrum antibiotics, later narrowed based on culture results, and for C. difficile infection with oral vancomycin. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV antibiotic therapy. His condition improved with normalization of liver function tests and negative blood cultures. He was discharged home with a two-week course of IV cefepime and tigecycline, oral vancomycin, and instructions for drain care and follow-up.
